replacement.title: Texas displacement and wartime refuge
replacement.text: The Tribe’s August 2012 history distinguishes several journeys. It places Waco and Tawakoni removal from the Brazos Reserve in 1859, with arrival in the Anadarko area on August 16; it says Wichita and Keechi had arrived a few days earlier from the Fort Arbuckle area. Its account later follows wartime flight to Kansas and return to village-building in Indian Territory. These are attributed retrospective histories, drawing on Elam’s book. They should not be flattened into one identical migration for every named people. The underlying removal reports and registers remain a research gap.

replacement.title: Reading path and the scope of this foundation
replacement.text: Begin with the Tribe’s connected history exhibit, then compare its more specific newsletter account of removal with the 1846 treaty text. Use the public dictionary and education pages as direct community-published routes. Harper’s trade-history pages, the collaborative twentieth-century study and Hodges’s language/archive case study ask different questions and should retain their dates, methods and perspectives. Further primary records, separately scoped affiliated histories and governing-text review remain open. This is a developing cited source guide, not a completed or community-endorsed history.

section.title: Reading the 1846 Council Springs treaty
section.text: The May 15, 1846 treaty names Wichita, Waco and other participating groups separately. Its text addresses trade, prisoners, violence, peace, and proposed blacksmith and teaching services. The printed signatory list also retains distinct period headings. Readers can examine a primary agreement here while keeping its limits clear: stated promises are not proof of implementation, and historical names or signatures alone do not settle present identity, jurisdiction or treaty rights.

sectionInsertions.afterTitle: A public route into the language

section.title: Language learning and community-controlled archives
section.text: Sapphire Hodges’s 2018 thesis examines archives and language-learning possibilities in a Wichita community setting. Her account describes Tribal direction of an archive project and argues for community control over learning priorities. The survey was largely voluntary at a local event, included people with different community relationships, and used self-assessed language ability. It is a dated case study, not a census or a test of present proficiency. The Tribe’s Department of Preservation separately describes its History Center, archives, library and language projects; listing a resource does not make all its materials public or establish learning outcomes.
